newsitem.title: CANADA: WTO rules against Canada on U.S. magazines.
newsitem.headline: WTO rules against Canada on U.S. magazines.

text.p: Canada's efforts to fend off what it perceives as a cultural onslaught from the United States has suffered a major setback in the form of a World Trade Organization ruling againstt the Canadian government's protectionist policies on magazines.

A confidential WTO decision, communicated to Ottawa and Washington on Thursday, ruled that Canada's attempts to protect the domestic magazine industry by taxing Canadian editions of U.S. magazines violated world trade rules.
In a move that placed the survival of some Canadian magazines in doubt, the WTO rejected other Canadian protectionist measures like preferential postal rates and tariff restrictions on magazines.
The decision was a slap in the face for the Liberal government of Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien and its cultural protectionist policies.
Canada has long feared for the survival of its fragile identity in the face of the cultural juggernaut of its much larger and more powerful southern neighbor.
Analysts said the Canadian government could either try to persuade the three-member WTO panel to reverse its decision at the last minute or appeal a final WTO judgement due next month.
However, trade analysts said chances of changing the ruling were slim.
"Frankly, I don't think either course will change the verdict," said Gerry Shannon, president of Ottawa-based Shannon Associates International Policy Consultants.
Instead, Ottawa may have to choose between new protectionist measures that would be acceptable under world trade rules or disregard Thursday's ruling and thus open the door for U.S. retaliation.
"The government is going to have to assess its position and find some other way to make sure that Canadians have access to Canadian writers and broadcasters," Shannon said.
Canada has long used cultural protectionist measures to curb the operations of U.S. television, print media and advertising, but few have succeeded.

Despite laws dating back to 1965 safeguarging Canada's publishing industry, up to 90 percent of Canada's cultural industry is dominated by U.S. films and publications, according to International Trade Minister Art Eggleton.
Giving U.S. magazines free access to the Canadian market could drive a number of Canadian publications out of business, media experts predicted.

"It will do some serious harm to Canadian publications. We will probably lose some of our smaller magazines. For all I know, we could lose some of our bigger magazines," said Ruth Biderman, executive director of the Canadian Periodical Writers Association.

Robert Lewis, editor of Maclean's weekly newsmagazine, Canada's answer to Time and Newsweek, said the WTO ruling could spell a significant loss of advertising revenues for Canadian magazines. That in turn, would mean less funds to cover Canadian stories.

"If foreign publications...scoop up a good chunk of that revenue, then yes, it is going to imperil the industry. There will be less money available for Canadian content and there may indeed be fewer magazines," Lewis said.
Thursday's decision was the latest chapter in a dispute that began in December 1995 when Ottawa imposed an 80 percent tax on advertising in U.S. magazines publishing Canadian editions.

The tax hit the Canadian edition of Sports Illustrated, owned by Time Warner Inc., particularly hard and in March 1996, the U.S. government took Washington's challenge of the controversial tax to the WTO.
Canadian International Trade Department spokesman Charles Larabie said on Friday that Canada was studying its options.

"We are still considering the report, and whether or not we are going to seek clarification or make an appeal remains to be seen," Larabie said. "There is still another month to go before the final report comes out."
"We'll be working very closely with the magazine industry to try and assess what we are going to do," he said.
